newsitem.title: USA: Hawaiian judge puts same-sex marriages on hold.
newsitem.headline: Hawaiian judge puts same-sex marriages on hold.

text.p: The judge who legalised gay and lesbian marriages in Hawaii put his historic ruling on hold on Wednesday while the state appealed the ruling to a higher court.

One day after unveiling his decision, Circuit Court Judge Kevin Chang sent the case, which would have made Hawaii the first state to allow same-sex marriages, to the Hawaiian Supreme Court at the request of state Deputy Attorney General Rick Eichor, who was expected to file a formal appeal later.

Eichor admitted during a court hearing before Chang on Wednesday that the chance of the state winning on appeal was "not particularly tremendous." But he urged the court to issue the stay nonetheless.
"Hundreds, perhaps thousands," of same-sex couples would get married if the stay was not granted before the appeal was heard, Eichor said. "The course of history will have forever changed," he added.
The state Supreme Court normally hears cases in the summer and makes its decision later that year or early the next year, meaning its ruling could come as late as 1998.

Attorney Dan Foley, representing three same-sex couples who filed the lawsuit in 1990 that led to Chang's ruling on Tuesday, told Chang his clients had been waiting to get married for six years and would have to wait another one to two years while the case was on appeal.
"It is our position that would be unjust," he said.
Foley later told Reuters he might ask for a reversal of the stay once the state had filed its appeal, or he might ask for the appeal hearing to be expedited immediately.
Chang said he was granting the stay in view of the "long history of this litigation and importance of these issues."
Meanwhile Chang's ruling on Tuesday revived the national debate on same-sex marriages, with those on both sides of the issue warning of a tough fight ahead.
As both sides formed battle lines on Wednesday, gay and lesbian activists were quick to caution against euphoria.

Evan Wolfson of the New York-based Lambda Legal Defence and Education Fund, a gay rights advocacy group, said Tuesday's ruling was "the beginning of the end for sex discrimination in marriage but ... in the meantime we still face backlash battles in several states."

Nowhere is the battle over gay and lesbian marriages likely to be fought harder than in California, where state Sen. Pete Knight vowed on Wednesday to reintroduce a bill in the state legislature that would block recognition of same-sex couples married in Hawaii.

"If we don't act soon, our public policy will be undermined when same-sex partners bring Hawaii marriage licenses back to this state and demand that their relationships be recognised as somehow equal to traditional marriage," the Republican said. Knight's bill was passed by the state Assembly last year but failed in the Senate.
Ellen McCormick of LIFE, a gay and lesbian activist organisation based in Sacramento, California, said she expected the state's laws to be tested if the Hawaii ruling is upheld.
"In order to have a case in California we need a couple to be married in Hawaii ... and then to return to California and ask the state to recognise their marriage," McCormick said.
